t49:
Ten minutes out. The base camp water tower is already visible above the treeline, rust-orange against the late afternoon sky.

You key the burner walkie — Reyes's frequency — and say it flat and calm, just one word:

"Rolling."

Static. Then nothing. Then a voice you don't recognize, careful and measured:

[Unknown voice: "Copy. Delivery confirmed?"]

You don't answer. You set the burner down on the passenger seat and let the silence work for you. Whoever's on the other end will either wait or panic. Either way, Marcus needs to hear that recording.

The base camp main gate comes into view ahead — chain-link and razor wire, and Marcus's silhouette already standing at the barrier. Even from two hundred yards you can see he's not alone. Three armed figures flank him, rifles up and ready. He called a reception committee.

Smart man.

You ease off the throttle, bring the cargo truck down to a crawl, and tap the headlights twice so Marcus knows it's you behind the wheel. Danny's pickup rolls up close behind, steady and tight.

Whatever comes next happens in the next sixty seconds. The gate is right there. Marcus's eyes are on the cab. And in the truck bed, Reyes shifts his weight — he knows exactly where he is.
t51:
The camp gate looms ahead in the dying amber light — the familiar chain-link and sandbag silhouette of home. Two armed guards wave you through without hesitation when they see the camp's cargo truck rolling in. They know the vehicle. They don't know what's in the back.

You pull up to the main staging area and kill the engine. Marcus is already there. He must have been watching the road for the last hour. His arms are crossed, jaw set, eyes moving across the cargo truck, the pickup, and then you — reading everything in two seconds flat.

He steps up to the driver's side as you drop out of the cab. Behind you, Danny kills the pickup's engine. The evening air carries dust and the faint smell of the camp cookfires.

Marcus: "You're back. All of you." His eyes flick to the truck bed. "That's Reyes."

Not a question.

You reach into your jacket and pull out the burner walkie-talkie — the one pulled from Reyes's pocket forty miles northwest. You hold it out to Marcus without a word.

His eyes drop to it. Then back up to you.

Marcus: "What is this?"

You tell him someone on the other end was in contact with Reyes. That it may still be active. That he needs to hear it himself.

Marcus takes the device slowly, turns it over in his thick hands. He studies the frequency setting — it's not the camp's band. His expression shifts from command-face into something harder and quieter. He keys the transmit button once. Holds it. Waits.

Static. Then nothing. Then — barely — a breath on the other end. Someone listening. Not speaking.

Marcus releases the button. The silence between you both is heavy as concrete. Whoever is on that frequency knows someone just keyed the walkie. And they know it wasn't Reyes.

Marcus pockets the burner. His voice drops low enough that only you hear it.

Marcus: "Get the prisoners into the storage shed. Nobody talks to them until I say so." A beat. "Then you and I are going to have a very long conversation."

Danny has the tailgate down already. The prisoners are being walked — not gently — toward the shed. Reyes doesn't look at Marcus. That tells you something.

The cargo truck sits silent and heavy in the staging area, its padlocked crates still unopened. The camp settles into its evening routine around you, most people unaware of what just rolled through the gate.

For the first time today, you're standing still. The mission is done. But whatever thread that burner walkie connects to — it's still live, still out there, and whoever holds the other end now knows something changed.
t53:
The cargo truck rolls through the main gate just as the last orange light bleeds out of the sky. Two of Marcus's men step aside without a word — they were expecting you. Word travels fast in a camp this small.

Marcus is already there. He stands at the edge of the gate, arms crossed, jaw tight. His eyes move from the cargo truck to Danny's pickup, then land on the three bound men in the bed. He doesn't react. Just takes it in.

You drop out of the cab and walk straight to him.

"Prisoners are intact. Cargo's intact. I want to open those crates — now. Together."

Marcus holds your gaze for a moment, then gives a short nod. He signals two of his men to pull the prisoners out and move them toward the storage shed. Reyes goes without a fight. The lean sentry stumbles. Nobody says anything.

Marcus pulls a pry bar from a nearby equipment rack and hands it to you without ceremony.

Marcus: "Your find, your call. Open it."

The first padlock comes off with bolt cutters from your toolbox. You wedge the pry bar under the crate lid and lean into it. Wood groans and splinters — then pops open.

Medical supplies. IV bags, sealed antibiotics, surgical kits still in sterile packaging. Enough to last the camp six months.

The second crate is heavier. You break it open and stare.

Fuel cells. Compact, military-grade. Twelve of them, foam-padded and labeled in stencil: **PROPERTY U.S. NATIONAL GUARD.**

Marcus goes very still beside you.

Marcus: "...Reyes knew where these were."

The silence between you says everything neither of you wants to say out loud yet.
t55:
Marcus listens without moving. He hasn't touched the manifest you handed him, hasn't looked at the crates, hasn't glanced at the prisoners since Danny marched them toward the storage shed. His entire attention is on you.

You keep your voice low — the kind of quiet that doesn't carry past two feet.

"He wasn't running. He had a plan. The warehouse, the fuel, the map — he was going to bring it all back. That means he understands logistics. He understands what this camp actually needs to survive."

Silence. The gate torches pop and hiss in the still night air.

Marcus finally exhales through his nose — slow and controlled, the way a man does when he's angry and choosing not to show it.

Marcus: "You're telling me the man who stole our only cargo truck, left a gate unlocked, and got two of my people killed... is an *asset.*"

It's not a question. His jaw is tight.

Marcus: "I hear you, Kevin. I do. But that decision isn't mine to make in the next five minutes. Right now Reyes sits in the shed and I think about what kind of example this camp needs."

He finally looks down at the map in his hands. His thumb traces the warehouse route.

Marcus: "But I'll tell you this — if that warehouse is real, and those supplies are real..." He folds the map once. "Then we talk about Reyes *after* we verify it."

His eyes come back up to yours. Hard, but not closed.
t57:
The Main Gate looms ahead under a clear night sky as you ease the cargo truck through. Marcus stands just inside the perimeter, arms crossed, two armed camp regulars flanking him. His eyes sweep the truck bed immediately — he counts three bodies, bound and alive — and something shifts behind his expression. Relief, maybe. Or calculation.

You kill the engine and step down from the cab. Danny pulls the pickup in behind you and cuts his lights.

Before Marcus can speak, you pull him aside. Low voice, close range.

"Reyes didn't defect. He was running a supply operation — unauthorized, but not treason. The two sentries?" You let that hang a beat. "Different story. They pulled weapons on camp personnel. That's a capital offense under your own rules, Marcus."

Marcus says nothing. He's listening.

"Reyes gets a chance to redeem himself. He knows the warehouse route, the frequency, the crates. We use him." You hold his gaze. "When he's done being useful — he had a tragic accident trying to flee. Far as anyone here knows, he was a hostage. We found him bound in the cab."

A long silence. A generator hums somewhere deep in the camp.

Marcus: "And the other two?"

You don't blink.

Marcus stares at you for three full seconds. Then he turns to his men and gives a quiet order you don't quite catch. The two regulars move toward the truck bed without being told twice.

Marcus looks back at you, voice flat and final.

Marcus: "The crates. I want them open. Now."
t59:
The crates hit the dirt in front of the main gate floodlights with a heavy thud. Someone found a bolt cutter — Marcus produced it without a word, like he'd been expecting this moment.

He crouches down and cuts the first padlock himself. The hasp springs open.

Silence from everyone in the yard — Danny, you, the two gate guards who caught wind something was happening and drifted over. Even Reyes, kneeling in the dirt with his wrists still bound, goes very still.

Marcus lifts the lid.

Inside, packed in military-surplus foam and plastic wrap: rifle ammunition. Hundreds of rounds, sorted by caliber. 5.56. 9mm. 12-gauge. Enough to last the camp six months at current consumption rates.

He opens the second crate without the bolt cutter — the padlock on this one is already cut from the outside. Military ration packs. Sealed, dated, untouched. Thirty of them at minimum.

Marcus doesn't speak for a long moment. He just looks at the contents, then slowly turns his gaze to Reyes.

Marcus: "You weren't running."

It isn't a question. His voice is flat and controlled, but there's something moving underneath it — recalculation. Reyes meets his eyes and says nothing, waiting.

Marcus stands up slowly, hands on his knees, and looks at you directly.

Marcus: "You brought me a traitor and a warehouse full of reasons to keep him alive. So. What's your read on this, Kevin?"

The gate guards are watching. Danny is watching. The answer you give right now shapes what happens to Reyes — and what happens to the camp.
t61:
The cargo truck rolls through the main gate just as the last light bleeds out of the sky. Floodlights snap on — Marcus must have had someone watching the road. He's standing twenty feet from the gate, arms crossed, two armed camp members flanking him. His eyes move from the cargo truck to Danny's pickup, then to the truck bed where three bound men are lying still.

He doesn't speak until you climb down from the cab and close the distance.

Marcus: "All three alive. Didn't expect that."

It's not quite a compliment. Not quite a question either. His jaw is tight, reading the situation before you say a word.

You lay it out flat. Reyes didn't run — he had a plan. Warehouse four miles north of the overpass, his cousin's place. Diesel, supplies, generator. He was going to come back. And he knows the route, the layout, the contacts. Lock him up and that knowledge rots with him. Put him to work on a supervised run and you might just solve the fuel problem before it solves you.

Marcus is quiet for a long moment. His eyes cut to Reyes in the truck bed, then back to you.

Marcus: "That's a hell of a pitch for a man who stole my truck."

He lets the silence stretch. Then — barely — his posture shifts.

Marcus: "Get them to the storage shed. I want Reyes separated from the other two. Nobody talks to him until I do."

He turns toward the cargo truck and the padlocked crates, his voice dropping.

Marcus: "And someone tell me what's in those boxes."
t63:
Marcus doesn't wait for an invitation. He pulls the bolt cutters from the equipment rack by the gate himself — the man clearly had them ready — and hands them to you without a word.

The first padlock takes two hard bites. It drops to the concrete with a clank.

You throw the crate lid open.

Military rations. Dozens of them. MRE pouches vacuum-sealed and stacked in tight rows, stamped with lot numbers and expiration dates two years out. Enough to feed Base Camp for a month, maybe six weeks if rationed hard.

The second crate is heavier. You feel it before you see it — the lid comes up and Marcus goes very still.

Medical supplies. IV bags. Antibiotics still in sealed pharmaceutical packaging. Surgical gauze, suture kits, a portable defibrillator still in its case. Whoever packed these crates knew exactly what a surviving settlement would need.

Marcus crouches slowly, picks up one of the antibiotic blister packs, and reads the label in the flashlight beam. His jaw is tight.

Marcus: "This didn't come from any cousin's warehouse."

He sets it down carefully. Stands. Looks toward the storage shed where Reyes is being held.

Marcus: "Reyes didn't steal from us. Someone *gave* him a shopping list."

The night air sits heavy between you both. Somewhere in the camp, a generator hums. The burner walkie-talkie in your pocket suddenly feels a lot heavier than it did forty miles ago.
t65:
The storage shed smells like motor oil and dried sweat. A single bare bulb flickers overhead, casting harsh shadows across the corrugated metal walls. Reyes sits on the concrete floor, back against a rusted shelving unit, wrists zip-tied behind him. His jaw is set, eyes tracking you the moment you push the door open.

You crouch down to his level. Close. No theatrics — just pressure.

**"The crates. The padlocked ones. Where did the supplies really come from, Reyes? And who else at camp knew?"**

He holds your gaze for a long moment. Then something behind his eyes shifts — not fear exactly. Calculation.

Reyes: "You think Marcus doesn't know where those crates came from? Ask him about the National Guard convoy that came through six weeks ago. Ask him why there's no record of it in the camp log." A dry, humorless laugh. "I didn't steal from the camp. I was moving what Marcus didn't want anyone to find."

He leans forward as far as the restraints allow.

Reyes: "The medical supplies — morphine, surgical kits, antibiotics. That's not surplus. That's black market. Someone with pull arranged that shipment before the grid went down, and Marcus has been sitting on it. Not distributing it. *Holding* it."

The bulb flickers. Outside, the camp is quiet.
t67:
The storage shed smells of motor oil, rust, and dried sweat. A single work lamp throws harsh yellow light across the concrete floor. Reyes sits with his back against a metal shelving unit, wrists zip-tied behind him, ankles bound with duct tape. He looks tired but alert — the kind of man who calculates even when he's losing.

You crouch down to his eye level. Close enough that he can't ignore you. Close enough that he can see the Glock resting on your knee.

"The crates. Where exactly are they hidden, and what does Marcus plan to do with them?"

Reyes holds the stare for a long moment. Then something shifts behind his eyes — not fear. Resignation.

Reyes: "You already opened them. You know what's inside."

He lets that hang.

Reyes: "Military-grade medical supplies. MREs. Antibiotics, IV bags, surgical kits. Enough to run a field hospital for six months. Marcus has been sitting on that cargo since week two of the outbreak. Won't distribute it. Won't explain why. Just — locked away."

He tilts his head toward the shelving unit behind him.

Reyes: "Proof? Check the inventory manifest. It's taped to the underside of the second crate. Marcus's signature is on it. His handwriting, his authorization code. He *signed* for those supplies and then made them disappear from the camp's records."

His jaw tightens.

Reyes: "People are getting sick out there, Kevin. People in *this* camp. And the man in charge is hoarding the cure."
t73:
You pull the burner walkie-talkie from your jacket pocket with one hand, keeping your eyes on the dark road ahead. The frequency is already set — whoever was listening before is probably still there.

You key the transmit button and drop your voice an octave. Steady. Authoritative.

"This is Marcus. We have a problem. Need to meet elsewhere. Respond."

Silence. Five seconds. Ten. The road hums under the cargo truck's tires.

Then static shifts — and a voice comes through. Male. Measured. The kind of calm that doesn't come naturally.

**Unknown Contact:** "...Marcus. Didn't expect to hear from you directly. What kind of problem?"

He's cautious. Probing. He hasn't confirmed a location or a name yet. Smart.

You've got maybe one or two exchanges before he figures out something's wrong. The voice doesn't sound like a scared civilian — it sounds like someone used to receiving bad news and deciding what to do about it.

In the rearview mirror, the camp gate lights appear on the horizon — maybe two miles out. You're almost home.

Whatever you say next, make it count.
